title: Staff pay and who held staff jobs
summary: Staff musicians took lower pay for security; staff jobs ran 120 players.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: We saw the loss, musicianwise, when the networks began to use the musicians, to pay staff instead of getting paid outside.

Right. Well, first off, the staff musicians got a lower pay than the outside musicians, but the consideration was it was a weekly salary and it was supposed to be a lifetime job, you know. Nobody foresaw that eventually they would cut down. And they had to employ 65 musicians for the networks and 30, I think, for the local stations. And places like CBS even hired -- when they had the symphony there -- I mean NBC, had 120, 130 musicians. So did CBS, and ABC had something like 120 musicians employed. And the local stations all had 30 musicians employed.
But they couldn't have been losing any money because they didn't pay commercially for all of the jobs.

Oh, no, they didn't lose money, no sir. But generally, the musicians who were on staff, they were good musicians, people who were trying to break into the commercial field, and the entrance to that would be through the staff orchestra.

There were also a lot of older musicians who just settled down in a comfortable job and just let time go by them. They didn't keep up too much, so that in general staff musicians in those days were sort of looked down on a little bit, the cream of the crop, that was to be what they called outside musicians, commercially paid musicians who made a living just from commercial programs, records and transcriptions.
